unesco.title: Mbende Jerusarema dance
unesco.description:
The Mbende Jerusarema Dance is a popular dance style practiced by the Zezuru Shona people living in eastern Zimbabwe, especially in the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe districts. 

The dance is characterized by acrobatic and sensual movements by women and men, driven by a polyrhythmic drummer accompanied by men playing woodblock clappers and by women handclapping, yodelling and blowing whistles. Unlike other drum-based East African dance styles, the Mbende Jerusarema does not rely on intricate foot stamping or a large number of drummers. Instead, the music is performed by one master drummer, and no songs or lyrics are involved. 

In the course of the dance, men often crouch while jerking both arms and vigorously kicking the ground with the right leg in imitation of a burrowing mole. The dance’s curious name reveals much about its vicissitudes over the centuries. Before colonial rule, this ancient fertility dance was called Mbende, the Shona word for “mole”, which was regarded as a symbol of fertility, sexuality and family. Under the influence of Christian missionaries, who strongly disapproved of this sexually explicit dance, the dance’s name was changed to Jerusarema, deriving from the Shona adaptation of the name of the city of Jerusalem, to endow it with a religious connotation. Both names are commonly used today. In spite of its condemnation by the missionaries, the dance remained popular and became a source of pride and identity in the struggle against colonial rule. 

The dance is changing its character and meaning as its enactment as an exotic animation for tourist audiences becomes more widespread. It is also increasingly used at political party rallies, where it is removed from all its original intentions. The mitumba drum, rattles and whistles, which used to accompany the dance, have successively been replaced by instruments of poor quality, contributing to the loss of the uniqueness of the Mbende music.

profile.name: Mbende Jerusarema
profile.tagline: A vigorous Zezuru Shona fertility dance that survived colonial bans under a biblical name.
profile.insight: Once banned by missionaries for its raw sexuality, this ancient Zezuru Shona mouse-and-mole dance survived by adopting the biblical name Jerusarema.
profile.profile: The Mbende Jerusarema is a traditional dance practiced by the Zezuru Shona people in eastern Zimbabwe, particularly in the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe districts. Characterized by acrobatic waist-shaking, sensual hip motions, and intense pelvic thrusts, it combines elements of a fertility, battle, and hunting dance. Originally called 'Mbende' after a fast-running mouse or mole, the dance was renamed Jerusarema under missionary pressure to give it a religious connotation. Today, it remains a powerful symbol of national pride, performed at weddings, funerals, and official state events.
profile.profile_long:
The Mbende Jerusarema dance is a prominent cultural tradition among the Zezuru Shona people of eastern Zimbabwe, specifically thriving within the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe districts. This ancient performance has traversed three distinct eras of Zimbabwean culture: the pre-colonial period before 1890, the colonial period from 1890 to 1980, and the post-colonial era from 1980 to the present day. Traditionally, the Zezuru community utilized Jerusarema for a variety of critical life events, including weddings, festivities, recreational competitions, funerals, and political meetings. Popular belief also holds that the Shona used the dance as a battle dance and a diversionary technique during military encounters, alongside its primary roles as a ritual fertility, hunting, and death dance.

The dance's original name, Mbende, translates to 'fast-running mouse' or 'mole', reflecting the animal's symbolism of rapidity, fertility, sexuality, and family. Rather than acting out a direct caricature, dancers project these animal traits through specific physical movements. Men frequently crouch while jerking both arms and forcefully kicking the ground with the right leg, mimicking a tunneling mole casting soil to the surface. Meanwhile, women engage in seductive, acrobatic waist-shaking and hip motions in sync with the men, culminating in intense pelvic thrusts directed toward each other that electrify the audience.

During the colonial era, Christian missionaries severely disapproved of the dance, mistaking its powerful pelvic movements for sexually graphic and suggestive behavior. Seeking to suppress it, the missionaries worked with village chiefs and local authorities to prohibit the dance in the early 20th century. However, village chiefs successfully petitioned to preserve the performance by renaming it Jerusarema—derived from the Shona adaptation of Jerusalem—to grant it a religious connotation associated with the birth of Jesus Christ. Despite this veneer of scripture, the dance retained its core identity and served as a powerful source of pride and resistance against colonial power. In 2005, UNESCO proclaimed the Mbende Jerusarema a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, followed by its inscription on the Representative List in 2008.

The auditory foundation of Mbende Jerusarema relies on a distinctive, polyrhythmic instrumentation that features no lyrics or singing. One master drummer—such as noted master percussionist Douglas Vembe—drives the rhythm using the mutumba drum, carved from the hard, resonant wood of the mutiti (Erythrina abyssinica) or mutsvanzwa (Pseudolachnostylis maprouneifolia) tree. This primary drum is accompanied by men playing wooden clappers (maja or manja) crafted from the durable mutara tree (Gardenia spathulifolia), alongside women handclapping, yodelling, and blowing whistles and rattles.

Material culture remains central to the tradition, particularly regarding clothing and instruments. Traditionally, dancers wore outfits made from the flexible, comfortable hides of wild animals such as leopards, monkeys, cheetahs, and wild cats, though modern practitioners increasingly blend textile fabrics with animal skins. Today, while the dance continues to be fiercely protected and practiced in rural clubs and urban gatherings, it faces new modern challenges. Its commercialization for tourist audiences and adaptation for official political rallies have occasionally stripped it of its traditional context, leading to the use of inferior instruments and altered meanings. Nevertheless, Mbende Jerusarema endures as an iconic pillar of Zimbabwean heritage.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated among the Zezuru Shona people of the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe districts in Mashonaland East. Performed across pre-colonial, colonial, and post-colonial eras, it began as an ancient fertility, military, hunting, and death ritual. Originally named Mbende after a burrowing mouse or mole, the dance was banned by Christian missionaries in the 1910s for its perceived lewdness. Village chiefs successfully negotiated its survival by renaming it Jerusarema after the city of Jerusalem. UNESCO recognized it as a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed in an open space with a line of musicians continuously playing and a group of men and women taking turns dancing. Women execute seductive, acrobatic waist-shaking and hip motions, while men crouch, jerk both arms, and vigorously kick the ground with the right leg like a burrowing mole. Both genders culminate their movements with intense pelvic thrusts directed toward each other. The music features no lyrics or intricate foot stamping.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is driven by a single master drummer playing the 'mutumba' drum, which is carved from the hard wood of the mutiti or mutsvanzwa tree for acoustic resonance. This is accompanied by men playing wooden clappers ('maja' or 'manja') made from the hard mutara tree, alongside women handclapping, yodelling, and blowing whistles and rattles.
sections.costume_and_setting: Traditional costumes were crafted from flexible wild animal skins, including leopard, monkey, cheetah, and wild cat leather, with domestic animal skins occasionally used as inferior alternatives. Modern dancers use a mixture of textile costumes and animal skins. It is performed at weddings, funerals, political rallies, festivals, and recreational competitions.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Mbende Jerusarema serves as a ritual fertility, celebration, memorial, and formerly a military diversion dance. It symbolizes family, sexuality, rapidity, and served as a crucial source of identity and pride in the resistance against colonial power. It is now featured at major national occasions.
sections.notable_figures: Douglas Vembe, a master drummer whose efforts contributed to the dance's inscription by UNESCO.
sections.regional_variants: Practiced widely across rural and urban districts of Zimbabwe, particularly centered in the Murewa and Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe (UPM) districts of Mashonaland East.
sections.lineage: Maintained by the Zezuru Shona ethnic group of eastern Zimbabwe as an unbroken living ancestral tradition.

profile.sacred_note: The dance began as an ancient fertility, hunting, and death ritual with deep spiritual status for the Zezuru Shona people, though colonial suppression and modern commercialization have shifted its public contexts.

basic_steps: Crouch and jerk both arms outward
Vigorously kick the ground with the right leg in imitation of a burrowing mole
Execute acrobatic waist-shaking and sensual hip motions
Culminate with intense pelvic thrusts directed toward a partner
teaching.rhythm: Polyrhythmic beat driven by a single master drum, woodblock clappers, rattles, and whistles with no lyrics
teaching.formation: A line of musicians playing continuously while a group of men and women take turns dancing in front of them
teaching.level_notes: Requires high physical stamina and core control, particularly for the men's grounded crouching kicks and the women's rapid hip and waist mobility.
